newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK- Lack of data may help bond mkt.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK- Lack of data may help bond mkt.

text.p: A sparsity of market-moving data in the coming week could provide much-needed relief to the fixed-income market as investors try to assess the economic situation after enduring large price losses.

The market sold off sharply on Friday following a nonfarm payrolls report that augured of inflationary wage pressures and continued strong job growth. Traders said an additional 25-basis-point tightening by the Federal Reserve's policy-making arm had already been built into prices. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets on May 20.

The most important economic release of the week, retail sales, won't hit until Friday along with producer prices, which were expected to have little impact. The Fed now is viewed as prepared to tighten despite weak producer or consumer price readings, analysts said.
February consumer credit was slated for release Monday and wholesale inventories on Tuesday. The Richmond Fed's March survey also was due Tuesday.
"The most that can hoped for is a pause of some sort that attracts some investor interest," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (U.S.A.) Co.

Strauss said it was likely that as much as 75 percent of the selloff ahead of an additional tightening already had taken place, leaving room for players to find profitable positions. Still, he expected to see two more tightenings by mid-summer.

He said some drop may be seen in energy and food prices this week, figures that may provide a "little bit of teasing to the market." The market also may see some short covering going into the week's numbers, he said. He also said the market could expect Fed officials to make plenty of statements indicating they believe last week's tightening was correct.

Unlike many other analysts economists at UBS expected the market to do the Fed's job by raising interest rates and slowing economic growth, thus relieving the central bank of the chore of tightening in May, Bostjancic said.
"But if the market doesn't tighten and the economy doesn't slow, then the Fed needs to come in in May," she said.

Traders expected Friday's payrolls report to continue to cast a pallor over the market going forward, however. Incipient signs of wage inflation were contained in the report and that was one indicator Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has warned he would closely watch.

Analysts also said the possibility of a coupon pass remained this week as strong tax inflows were pressuring the open market desk to add permanent reserves via outright Treasuries purchases to offset tax-related shortfalls that mount after mid-month.

Late Friday the 30-year Treasury bond was trading at 93-26/32 to yield 7.13 percent. The 10-year was at 95-10/32 to yield 6.91 percent. The five-year was at 99-14/32 to yield 6.76 percent and the two-year was at 99-22/32 to yield 6.42 percent.
Three-month bills were at 5.14 percent; six-month bills at 5.32 percent and year bills at 5.63 percent.

Economists polled by Reuters expected, on average, retail sales would rise 0.6 percent in March, down from the prior month's 0.8 percent increase. Excluding autos, they saw a rise of 0.4 percent. Producer prices were seen remaining unchanged.
"It's going to be quiet with not much in the way of important news until Friday," said Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities Inc. "There's not much new on the fundamental scene."
Treasury's auction of 10-year inflation-indexed bonds on Tuesday wasn't expected to have much impact, she said, and trading could be technically driven much of the week.
